h1: Cellar and packaging jobs: where most brewers start
title: Cellar and Packaging Jobs in a Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: What cellar and packaging jobs in a brewery involve, the skills they teach and why most professional brewers in India started on one of them.
teaser: The brewhouse gets the photos. The cellar and the packaging line are where most brewers actually learn the job.
standfirst: Ask a head brewer where they started and the answer is usually the cellar or the canning line. These jobs are hard work but they teach the parts of brewing that decide whether a beer reaches the customer in good shape.
sections: Why the first job is rarely the brewhouse

Brewing a batch takes one day. Fermenting, conditioning, carbonating and packaging it can take weeks. Most of a brewery's labour and most of its risk sit after the brew day, so that is where the entry level jobs are.

Cellar and packaging roles are also where a brewery can safely train someone. A mistake on the brewhouse can ruin a batch in an hour. Mistakes in the cellar happen more slowly, with a senior person close by to catch them.

The cellar is the fermentation and conditioning area. A cellar operator looks after the beer while the yeast works and after it has finished:

  • Taking daily gravity and temperature readings and logging them.
  • Harvesting yeast from the bottom of fermenters for the next batch.
  • Dry hopping, often by climbing onto a tank with a bag of pellets.
  • Transferring finished beer to a bright tank and carbonating it.
  • Cleaning and sanitising every vessel, hose and fitting, repeatedly.

A typical precise task: carbonating a lager in the bright tank at around 1 °C to about 2.5 volumes of carbon dioxide. Cold beer holds gas far better than warm beer, so the same pressure at the wrong temperature gives you a flat or a foaming product.

Packaging means kegging, canning or bottling. In a brewpub it might be one person filling kegs on a manual filler. In a production brewery it is a line with a crew, running for a full shift with targets for output and quality.

The skill that matters most is keeping oxygen out. Every time beer splashes or a can sits open too long before seaming, it picks up oxygen and starts to go stale. Packaging staff who understand this and check fill levels and seams without being asked are worth a great deal to a brewery that ships beer across India's heat.

Cellar work teaches yeast behaviour, fermentation timing and hygiene, the three things that decide most beer faults. Packaging teaches oxygen control, carbonation and the discipline of running to a schedule. A brewer who has done both understands why a recipe that looks perfect on paper can still fail in the market.

It is also where you learn whether you like the work. It is physical, often hot, frequently wet and involves shifts. If you still want to brew after a year of this, you probably will.

Breweries hiring for these roles look for reliability, physical fitness, safety sense and a basic understanding of what is going on in the tanks. An internship helps a lot: see our guide to getting a brewery internship in India. A homebrewing record helps too, as long as you present it honestly.

The common weak spot is the theory. Candidates can lift kegs but cannot explain why fermentation temperature matters or what a diacetyl rest is for. Fixing that before an interview is one of the quickest ways to stand out.

Cellar shifts usually start early. You check every fermenter's temperature and pressure, take samples and log gravity readings so the brewer can decide what moves that day. Then comes the planned work: a transfer from fermenter to bright tank, a yeast harvest, a dry hop addition or a full clean of an emptied vessel.

Packaging shifts are set by the schedule. You set up the filler, sanitise every contact surface, purge kegs or cans with carbon dioxide and run the batch. A colleague or the QC team checks fill levels, seams and dissolved oxygen as you go. The last hour is cleaning the line so it is ready for tomorrow.

Expect wet floors, cold rooms and the smell of sanitiser. Expect to finish tired. Most brewers remember these shifts with surprising affection, because this is where the job started to make sense.

From the cellar the usual step is to assistant brewer, then brewer, then head brewer. From packaging some people move into brewing, others into packaging management, maintenance or quality control. Either way you will carry a working knowledge of the parts of brewing that many recipe writers never learn properly.
faqs: Do cellar jobs require brewing experience?
Not usually. Breweries hire for reliability and attitude, then train on the job, though basic brewing knowledge makes you much quicker to trust.
Is packaging a dead end in a brewery?
No. Many brewers started on the packaging line. Oxygen control and carbonation are skills every head brewer needs.
Quite physical. Expect lifting, climbing onto tanks, dragging hoses and long periods standing on wet floors, so good boots and safe lifting habits matter.
